Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
There is something wrong with me as a person
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette:
Mai was thirty-two when the abuse began, and she did not recognise it for what it was until much later. Her partner had always been intense, but the first time he grabbed her wrist and forced her to her knees, she told herself it was a misunderstanding. He was angry about something she had said—she could not remember what—and he wanted her to apologise. When she hesitated, he pressed an ice pack from the freezer against the back of her neck and held it there, saying she needed to cool down. She stayed frozen, not because of the cold but because she believed that if she moved, he would hurt her more. That moment—the specific sensation of that cold pressure, the feeling of having no choice, the grip of his hand—became a template for everything that followed.

Over the next year, the incidents multiplied. He would trap her in rooms, demand she repeat apologies, grab her arm when she tried to leave. She learned to comply. But the memory never felt like something in the past. When she was triggered—a patient’s hand on her shoulder, the chill of a therapy ice pack, a supervisor telling her to change a treatment plan—the scene would return as if it were happening again. Her chest would tighten, her vision would narrow, and she would need to excuse herself to the staff bathroom, where she would sit on the floor until the shaking stopped. She could never explain what happened if a colleague asked. The words would tangle, and she would trail off, overwhelmed by a rush of emotion that left her silent.

Mai began to avoid. She stopped accepting evening shifts because the parking lot felt unsafe. She requested to work only with female patients, though she could not say why. When a male patient needed hands-on therapy, she felt a flash of heat and dread, and she would hand him off to a coworker with a vague excuse about her schedule. At home, she avoided her husband’s touch in certain ways—flinching when he reached for her, sleeping on the far edge of the bed. He did not know about the abuse; she had never told him. She was certain that if he knew, he would see her the way she saw herself: defective, humiliated, someone who had failed to prevent what happened.

The self-blame was relentless. She replayed the arguments, the moments before the ice pack, the times she could have left. She dwelled on the person she used to be—confident, easy with her hands, quick to laugh—and saw her current self as a stranger. She was vigilant in every room, scanning for men who seemed angry or controlling, cataloguing exits. The rumination about prevention exhausted her: if only she had not said that, if only she had left earlier, if only she had been stronger. She believed the abuse had happened because of the way she acted, and that belief made the world feel dangerous in a way she could not control.

The consequences accumulated. Her supervisor noticed she was avoiding certain patients and asked if she was burned out. Mai said yes. Her marriage grew distant. She stopped meeting friends for dinner. The hypervigilance bled into her sleep, and she woke each morning already tired. What finally brought her to therapy was a moment at work: a patient with a mild stroke needed passive range of motion on his left arm, and when Mai took his hand, the temperature of his skin—cool, slightly damp—sent her straight back to the kitchen floor, the ice pack, the grip. She froze for several seconds, then excused herself and vomited in the bathroom. That evening, she searched online for a trauma therapist and made an appointment.

She is afraid of what she will find in the memories she has tried so hard to contain. But she is also afraid of staying as she is—of losing her career, her marriage, the last pieces of the person she used to be. She hopes the therapy will help her stop living in a moment that already ended, though she cannot yet imagine how that would feel.
